newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Positive note struck in Israel, Palestinian talks.
newsitem.headline: Positive note struck in Israel, Palestinian talks.

text.p: Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation failed in talks on Wednesday to reach any agreement on thorny issues, but Israel's chief negotiator said at least mutual accusations were set aside.
A Palestinian negotiator, who said Israel was now studying his side's proposals for increased security in the West Bank town of Hebron when Israeli troops redeploy, sounded a note of optimism.
"Apparently the Israelis have come to understand that the (Hebron) agreement has to be adhered to and they are studying the agreement," Hassan Asfour told Reuters.

"A serious and detailed discussion has taken place," an Israeli participant at the meetings in the Palestinian self-rule enclave in the Gaza Strip quoted Israeli delegation head Dan Shomron as saying.
Shomron said no agreement had been reached but "mutual accusations had been laid aside".
Palestinian delegation head Saeb Erekat said earlier on Wednesday the Hebron talks, which opened on Sunday, were deadlocked.
Fifty-nine Arabs and 15 Israelis died in an outbreak of violence last month, largely prompted by Palestinian frustration over the slow pace of the peace process.

"One of the easy solutions to the security concerns of Israelis who are trying to change the Hebron agreement under the pretext of offering additional security...is to move settlers from the city centre to the nearby Kiryat Arba settlement," Erekat told Reuters before Wednesday's talks ended.
Some 400 Jews live amidst 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron and 5,500 Israelis live in adjacent Kiryat Arba.
Erekat, who had said the Israeli negotiators were trying to rewrite the agreement signed by a previous Israeli government, was cautious after Wednesday's talks.

"I think that we made it very, very clear to the Israelis that the agreement cannot be changed...I really hope, and I'm not sure whether they got the message...but I really hope that the Israeli side will really start doing business and implement the agreement."

Asfour said Palestinian proposals to beef up security in Hebron after Palestinian police entered the town under the deal included running joint Israeli-Palestinian patrols and more of them in the city.

"The Israeli side is studying Palestinian proposals to set up a security system that is consistent with the agreement and does not change the agreement and maintains security for both sides," Asfour said.
Israel agreed more than a year ago to redeploy in Hebron by March of this year but delayed the process after Palestinian suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took office in June after May elections. Most Palestinians say they doubt his pledge to keep to the signed peace accords.

Palestinian officials had said earlier that the Israeli delegation to the Hebron talks proposed changes that would reduce the number of Palestinian police allowed in Hebron and insisted they be armed with pistols rather than rifles.
The Israelis also wanted to keep control of parts of the town due to be transferred to the Palestinians under the existing agreement, which the Jewish settlers oppose.
Erekat argued that Palestinians had their own security concerns because of the militant settlers. A Jewish settler massacred 29 Palestinian worshippers at Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque in 1994.
Talks resume on Thursday in the Israeli-controlled area of Gaza near the border with the Jewish state.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, mediating at the talks, said: "They are making a serious effort to understand each other's concerns."
